043 - The Golden Compass and Philosophy: Philip Pullman's His Dark Materials trilogy, beginning with The Golden Compass (1995), is a celebrated fantasy series about the girl Lyra, her shape-shifting dæmon, and a journey across parallel worlds to overthrow 'the Authority' himself. The books are famously controversial for attacking organized religion, which makes them rich ground for philosophy: whether Pullman's god is really the God of the philosophers, whether lying and storytelling can be virtues, what the soul-splitting of children says about belief, and whether heresy corrupts young readers or teaches them to think.
044 - Led Zeppelin and Philosophy - All: Led Zeppelin, the English hard-rock band of the late 1960s and 1970s behind 'Stairway to Heaven' and 'Whole Lotta Love', were dismissed by critics as blues thieves and purveyors of mere excess, yet their occult imagery and myth-soaked lyrics were the work of serious spiritual seekers. Their music raises real philosophical questions: whether their thunderous sound is an experience of the sublime, how a band creates as a group, whether uncredited borrowings undermine their authenticity, and why their lyrics so often demean women.
045 - World of Warcraft and Philosophy -: World of Warcraft, Blizzard's massively multiplayer online game running since 2004, lets millions of players quest, raid, and trade in the fantasy world of Azeroth. The world is virtual but the people are real, and that gap generates genuine philosophy: is killing players at an in-game funeral murder or fair play, does the auction house model perfect market economics, can a game answer nihilism, and does a character controlled entirely from above have free will? The book itself is framed like a quest log.
046 - Mr. Monk and Philosophy - The Curi: Mr. Monk, the USA Network comedy-drama (2002-2009), stars Tony Shalhoub as Adrian Monk, a brilliant detective whose obsessive-compulsive disorder is both the 'gift and curse' behind his casework and the ruin of his daily life. The show is a goldmine for philosophy: Monk as Camus's happy Sisyphus in a war on dirt he can never win, his phenomenological way of seeing what the rest of us miss, whether his epiphanic certainty about whodunit is justified, and what his halting friendships reveal about Aristotle's virtues.
047 - Anime and Philosophy - Wide Eyed W: Anime, Japanese animation, ranges from the giant-robot violence of Akira and Neon Genesis Evangelion to the gentle spirits of My Neighbor Totoro, and it is emphatically not children's fare. Its shape-shifting bodies, cyborgs, and uploaded minds make it perhaps the richest medium for asking what a person is: is Motoko of Ghost in the Shell still herself when she merges with the net, is the monstrous Tetsuo of Akira still Tetsuo, and are we already cyborgs anyway? The book reads these stories through posthuman theory, gender, and tragedy.
048 - The Red Sox and Philosophy - Green: The Boston Red Sox are baseball's great tragedy-to-triumph story: for eighty-six years after selling Babe Ruth to the Yankees, the team broke its fans' hearts in increasingly improbable ways, until the miracle 2004 championship changed everything. That history makes fandom itself a philosophical subject: how to govern the emotions a game provokes, what makes an authentic rather than bandwagon fan, whether losing teaches what winning cannot, and what the curse's end did to a community long glued together by shared doom.
049 - Zombies, Vampires, and Philosophy: The twenty-first century has seen a boom in the Undead, from Twilight and True Blood to zombie walks and Romero-style splatter films, and this book asks why these monsters in particular fascinate us. The vampire, a superhuman predator charged with guilt, and the zombie, dead flesh that shambles beyond all morality, let philosophers probe personal identity (would it be me rising?), whether Undeath could really be worse than death, whether the Undead can be evil, and what the philosophical-zombie thought experiment owes to its fictional namesakes.
050 - Facebook and Philosophy - What's o: Facebook, the social network launched in 2004, now shapes how billions of people friend, post, and perform their lives online, and this book takes that everyday apparatus seriously. Chapters ask whether trivial status updates can still matter, how the site breaks the old 'know your audience' rule of privacy, whether a Facebook friend is an Aristotelian friend, whether profiles foster authenticity or a surrogate self that mourns on our behalf, and whether users' unpaid posts amount to digital labor in a walled garden.
051 - Soccer and Philosophy - Beautiful: Soccer, the world's most popular sport, rests on one rule: move the ball into the net without using your hands. From that simplicity the book derives big questions: why a ball crossing an arbitrarily drawn line ignites passions on every continent, whether the 'best' team can really lose (and what that even means), how luck, injustice, and drama make the game a rehearsal for life, what Nietzsche would make of Arsenal, and why a beautiful goal might be a moral as well as an aesthetic achievement.
053 - Martial Arts and Philosophy - Beat: This book is not about one pop-culture work but about the world's fighting traditions - karate, kendo, judo, boxing, fencing, and the Shaolin Temple - which have always sat close to philosophy: Plato wrestled, and Zen shaped the samurai swordsmanship of writers like Takuan Soho. The essays ask what a black belt actually certifies, whether dojo courtesy could ever matter in a real fight, how a kendo master can strike without thinking, whether the self that martial training masters even exists, and what Buddhist no-self does for compassion in combat.
